quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.exhaustive_search_summary: Only the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage) has been searched for q_001. Post-1860 censuses, probate, church, and vital records have not yet been searched.
items.narrative_markdown: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 census in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Co-enumeration is indirect evidence that supports but does not prove parentage. Post-1860 censuses, probate, and church records have not yet been searched.

items.rationale: 1850 census fully indexed on FamilySearch. Free access, start here.
Ancestry has independent indexing; cross-check for transcription errors.
Third independent index for coverage confirmation.

entry.rationale: Ancestry 1870 United States Federal Census (ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/) — name-searchable. Specifically requested for this plan. Patrick Flynn born ~1845 would be approximately 25 in 1870; Thomas Flynn born ~1818 would be approximately 52. If Patrick still lived with Thomas, the household entry establishes co-residence one decade after the 1860 co-enumeration already in the tree (S2). If Patrick had formed his own household, the entry records his birth state, corroborating or correcting the Ireland vs. Pennsylvania discrepancy between the tree's birth fact and the project objective. Thomas's own entry may list other children who can be searched as siblings.

FamilySearch collection 1438024 (United States Census, 1870) — name-searchable. Same census year as pli_004 but independently indexed; use if the Ancestry transcription missed the entry or produced a different spelling. Also search under Thomas Flynn directly to find his 1870 household, which may list children not found under Patrick's search.

FamilySearch collection 1417683 (United States Census, 1880) — name-searchable. The 1880 census is the first to record each person's relationship to the head of household, making it the strongest census year for parentage. Thomas Flynn born ~1818 would be approximately 62 if still alive; Patrick approximately 35. If Thomas and Patrick appear in the same household with an explicit 'son' relationship, that is stronger evidence than the indirect co-enumeration the 1850 and 1860 censuses supply. Even if Thomas has died by 1880, Patrick's entry records birthplace and parents' birthplaces.

FamilySearch collection 1325221 (United States Census, 1900) — name-searchable. Patrick Flynn born ~1845 would be approximately 55 in 1900 and died 1908-03-12, so this is his last full census year. The 1900 schedule records year of immigration, number of years in the U.S., and parents' birthplaces — all contextual corroboration. It may also identify a wife whose marriage record (pli_008) can supply the mother's maiden name. Patrick's death cert (S3) is already in the tree; this census extends the documented record chain to within eight years of his death.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records — name-searchable. Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother. This record: (a) confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple before Patrick's birth; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which census records and the 1908 death certificate (S3) typically omit; (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845), corroborates Thomas as father where the parentage currently rests on indirect co-enumeration alone. Date range set to Thomas's plausible marriage years given his birth ~1818. Note: the couple's marriage proves they were married — it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child; a record placing Patrick with them (1850/1860 census) must accompany it. The loc_001 locality entry notes Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia through the period; try variant spellings Flyn, Flinn, Flynn.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 — browse-only (personCount 0). Image browse of Schuylkill County probate dockets for Thomas Flynn. Thomas born ~1818 could plausibly have died anywhere from the mid-1850s through roughly 1910; date range is bounded by Thomas's plausible lifespan as the record's creator, not by Patrick's research window. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence. The loc_001 locality entry notes probate records are held by the county Register of Wills and are available from 1811. Because personCount is 0, this requires image-by-image browsing of the county dockets rather than a name search.

FamilySearch collection 1910717 (United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865) — name-searchable. Patrick Flynn born ~1845 would have been 16–20 during the Civil War, reaching enlistment age by 1862–1863. A service or pension record often states birthplace, occupation, and next of kin, providing contextual corroboration of origin (Ireland vs. Pennsylvania) and potentially identifying a Thomas Flynn as beneficiary or contact — indirect evidence of the father-son relationship. This also covers the possibility that military service took Patrick out of Schuylkill County during the 1860–1870 intercensal period, explaining any absence from the 1870 census (pli_004/pli_005).

FAN item — required for a parentage question. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records — name-searchable. Search for other children of Thomas Flynn whose baptism or burial records name both Thomas and his wife. A sibling's baptism entry that explicitly names both parents is direct evidence of Thomas's paternity and supplies the mother's maiden name as a cross-check against pli_008. The godparents and witnesses named in those entries are also FAN leads — persons who may appear in adjacent census households or land records and confirm family structure. Date range spans the period when Thomas (born ~1818) would plausibly have had children baptized.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate is already in the project tree as source S3 (collection 2255317, name-searchable) and cited on the ParentChild relationship between I1 and I2, but no assertion for q_001 has been drawn from it for parental information. Pennsylvania death certificates filed from 1906 include fields for father's name, father's birthplace, mother's maiden name, and mother's birthplace. Even if the informant's knowledge is limited — Patrick was an Irish immigrant — any name or birthplace stated is a direct lead. The loc_001 locality guide confirms statewide civil death registration began in 1906; Patrick's 1908 death falls within that system. This is the fastest and most direct route to a parental statement.

The 1880 US census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) is the first to state each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. Patrick would be approximately 35 in 1880. If Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, then ~62) is still alive in Schuylkill County, Patrick may appear in his household listed as 'son' — a direct relationship statement far stronger than the inferred 1850 co-enumeration. Even if Patrick heads his own household by 1880, the census records his father's and mother's birthplace, pointing to the Irish county of origin and enabling Irish church record searches. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Knowing which county he lived in before 1882 reveals the distance and direction of the migration and may show family members who later moved together. The United States Census, 1880 (name-searchable) is the census straddling the stated 1882 move. If Michael appears in Schuylkill County in 1880, the move predated 1882; if elsewhere, the actual move window narrows to 1880-1882. Crucially, Patrick Sheahan (I2) purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (Deed Book 42, p. 118, source S1). Searching Patrick in the 1880 census confirms whether he was established in Schuylkill County before Michael arrived, directly testing the hypothesis that Michael followed an already-settled sibling. Search both 'Sheahan' and 'Sheehan' for each brother.

The United States Census, 1900 (name-searchable) would show Michael established in Schuylkill County roughly 18 years after the move. The 1900 schedule records birthplace, parents' birthplaces, and years married — supplementing what other records may not capture. If Michael is listed as a miner in 1900, that confirms sustained coal-mining employment consistent with the work-driven-migration hypothesis. The census may also show Patrick Sheahan in a nearby household, further testing the sibling-settlement pattern. Try 'Sheehan' as a variant.

The United States Census, 1910 (name-searchable) adds the 'employer, employee, or own account' column absent from the 1900 schedule. If Michael is listed as an employee of a named mine or company, that is specific corroboration of coal-mining employment and may identify which company drew him to the county. This item is a fallback for pli_003 if the 1900 record is not found, and also independently covers the decade following 1900.

Pennsylvania civil death registration began in 1906. If Michael died between 1906 and 1968, the Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 collection (name-searchable) would record his birthplace, parents' names, occupation, and length of Pennsylvania residence — fields most census records do not supply. The birthplace field would directly confirm whether Michael was an Irish immigrant, and the occupation field would confirm sustained coal-mining employment. The informant's testimony about his parents may also name the Irish county of origin, clarifying whether the Schuylkill County move was part of a wider chain-migration pattern. Try 'Sheehan.'

Roman Catholic parishes served the Irish mining community in Schuylkill County. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (name-searchable) covers 1708-1985. A sacramental record for Michael — a marriage, the baptism of a child, or a family member's burial — would date his first appearance in a local parish and may bracket the actual move year more tightly than the 1882 estimate. Some Irish immigrant parish registers note the baptismal place of origin; if present, that would identify Michael's county of origin in Ireland. These fields directly test the chain-migration hypothesis: if Michael arrived in the United States before 1875 and lived elsewhere before moving to Schuylkill County, the naturalization file documents that intermediate step, separating his US immigration from his Schuylkill County relocation.

Pennsylvania's Bureau of Mines published annual reports from 1870 onward listing every mine in operation in Schuylkill County, numbers of workers employed, and mine fatalities with individual names. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Research Plan for q_001: Who were the parents of María Josefa García Romero?**

Mode: **Create** — plan pl_001 written for q_001.

---

**What's already known about the subject (I1):**
- Birth: about 1843, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain (unsourced)
- No parents, spouse, children, or cited sources in the tree

---

**Plan pl_001 — 8 items in execution order:**

1. **pli_001** — *Baptism, indexed search, FamilySearch* (1841–1845): Search "Spain, Baptisms, 1502–1940." The Santa María volume for 1841–1845 is 96% name-indexed. Baptism entries name both parents and all four grandparents; García = father's surname, Romero = mother's maiden surname per Spanish double-surname convention.

2. **pli_002** — *Baptism, full-text fallback, FamilySearch* (1837–1850): If pli_001 fails, search the same Santa María registers via FTS using García + Romero as required co-occurrence terms (image group 004104131, not fully indexed).

3. **pli_003** — *Baptism, Ancestry fallback* (1841–1845): Ancestry's Spain, Select Baptisms, 1502–1940 (collection 60164), as a paid-repository fallback if both FamilySearch paths return nothing.

4. **pli_004** — *Marriage, indexed, FamilySearch* (1820–1843): Search "Spain, Marriages, 1565–1950" for a García man × Romero woman. Confirms the parental couple and supplies the mother's maiden surname; corroborates the father by date.

5. **pli_005** — *Marriage, broader fallback, FamilySearch* (1800–1850): "Spain, Catholic Church Records, 1307–2005," covering pre-marriage files and registers not in the specialized index.

6. **pli_006** — *Siblings' baptisms, FamilySearch* (1830–1860): Search for other García/Romero children in the same parish; a sibling's baptism independently names the same parents and corroborates parentage. Godparents are FAN leads.

7. **pli_007** — *Census/padrón, FamilySearch* (1840–1871): "Spain, Málaga, Municipal Records, 1760–1956" — municipal census registers that could place the subject in a García household before civil registration began in 1871.

8. **pli_008** — *Death records, FamilySearch* (1843–1905): "Spain, Deaths, 1600–1920" for the father (García) and mother (Romero); death entries may name spouse and children.

---

**Fallback chains:**
- Baptism: pli_001 → pli_002 → pli_003
- Marriage: pli_004 → pli_005

**8 searches total** across FamilySearch and Ancestry (free collections first).

---

**Next step:** Execute **pli_001** with the **search-records** agent (FamilySearch indexed name search for the 1843 baptism). Confirm before proceeding.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

- Military service 1862–1865, Indiana, United States
- Death 1879, Vigo County, Indiana, United States

**Plan pl_001 — 8 items in execution order:**

- **pli_001** — census, United States (nationwide), 1850, FamilySearch — The 1850 census covers all states; one search reaches both Indiana and Ohio results. - **pli_002** — census, United States, 1850, Ancestry — fallback for pli_001 — Ancestry's independently keyed 1850 index; a name badly garbled in one index may appear in the other.
- **pli_003** — census, United States (focus Indiana / Vigo County), 1860, FamilySearch — The 1860 census. Josiah was ~32 and enlisted in Indiana two years later, making Vigo County the likely 1860 location. All co-residents recorded for follow-up.
- **pli_004** — census, United States, 1860, Ancestry — fallback for pli_003 — Independent keying; covers what FamilySearch may miss.
- **pli_005** — military, Indiana, 1862–1865, Fold3 — Compiled military service record names the enlistment county, regiment, company, and often a next-of-kin or home address. Covers the portion of the question window the census snapshots miss.
- **pli_006** — military, United States, 1861–1934, FamilySearch — Civil War and Later Pension Files. Pension applications contain stated residence, depositions naming family members and witnesses from both the war years and earlier.
- **pli_007** — tax, Vigo County, Indiana, 1849–1865, Indiana State Archives — Annual tax lists narrow the year Josiah arrived in Vigo County. Adjacent landowner names (FAN). Unindexed; must be requested from Indiana State Archives.
- **pli_008** — vital_record (marriage), Vigo County, Indiana, 1849–1865, Vigo County Clerk of Courts — If Josiah married during the window, the marriage record names his spouse (direct "with whom" answer) and witnesses (FAN). Unindexed; must be requested from the county clerk.

The census names co-residents but states no relationships between them (loc_001 quirk), so household composition provides indirect evidence of family ties. Search variant spellings — Roe, Row, Rowe — to account for indexing errors.

Ancestry maintains an independently keyed 1850 census index (the external collections stored for Vigo County include Ancestry's US federal census collection). If the FamilySearch search (pli_001) yields no match or an ambiguous result under any spelling variant, Ancestry's separate keying may surface a differently indexed entry for the same household.

entry.jurisdiction: United States (focus on Indiana, especially Vigo and neighboring counties)
entry.rationale: The 1860 federal census is the second snapshot within the question window. Josiah was ~32 in 1860; two years later he enlisted in Indiana, strongly suggesting he was in Indiana — likely Vigo County — by 1860. The locality guide (loc_001) lists this as collection 1473181, name-searchable nationwide. The 1860 schedule names all household members with ages and birthplaces. The census states no relationships (loc_001 quirk), so all co-residents should be recorded for follow-up. Search variant spellings and prioritize Indiana results.

Ancestry's independently keyed 1860 census index is a fallback if the FamilySearch search (pli_003) is inconclusive or returns an ambiguous match. Ancestry and FamilySearch use different transcription vendors for the 1860 census, so a name that is missed or badly garbled in one index may appear in the other.

The tree records Josiah's military service 1862–1865, enlisted in Indiana. His compiled military service record (CMSR) would name the county of enlistment, the regiment, and the company, placing him geographically for 1862 and throughout the war. The enlistment record often names a next of kin or home residence. The external collections stored for Vigo County include Fold3 for military records; NARA holds the original CMSRs and Fold3 is the primary online access point. This covers the 1862–1865 portion of the question window that the census snapshots miss.

The locality guide for Vigo County (loc_001) lists collection 1888129 (United States Civil War and Later Pension Files, 1861–1934) as a resource for the period. Pension files typically contain the veteran's stated residence, declarations naming family members and witnesses, and depositions covering both the war years and earlier. A pension application could name co-residents or family members present during the question window. This item is searched after the CMSR (pli_005) because the pension file extends the CMSR's leads into family and residence detail.

Annual county tax lists track when a person first appears in the county, providing a proxy for arrival that the census cannot — census snapshots are a decade apart, so tax lists narrow the migration year if Josiah moved from Ohio to Vigo County during the question window. The locality guide (loc_001) notes Indiana probate and land records for Vigo County are not indexed in a surfaced collection and must be accessed through the Indiana State Archives or the county. Tax lists may also name adjoining property owners (FAN context) and corroborate or contradict the census household picture.

If Josiah married during the question window, a marriage record would establish a new household and name his spouse — a direct answer to 'with whom was he living.' The locality guide (loc_001) notes Indiana marriage records for Vigo County are not indexed in a surfaced collection and should be requested from the county clerk or Master Commissioner; Indiana had no statewide vital registration before 1882 (loc_001 quirk). A marriage record would also date the household formation, complementing the decade-apart census snapshots. Witnesses named on the bond or license are FAN leads.

The 1850 census (sequence 1-2) establishes baseline location; 1860 census (sequence 3-4) narrows to Indiana; military records (sequence 5-6) cover the service window; tax records (sequence 7) fill the decade gap; marriage records (sequence 8) complete the household picture. Date ranges reach the later part of the question window: the pension file's 1861-1934 range extends past 1865 to capture affidavits about the earlier period. No item depends on evidence only a later item can supply.

dimensions.name: Jurisdiction accuracy
dimensions.rationale: Jurisdictions are historically accurate for the 1850-1865 period. Vigo County, Indiana existed from 1818-present per loc_001. Ohio is correctly named for the birth location. The plan correctly notes that Indiana had no statewide vital registration before 1882, so county records are the appropriate jurisdiction for marriage records. No anachronistic jurisdictions or pre-statehood errors appear.

dimensions.name: Plan mode and lifecycle
dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly chose 'create' mode for the first plan on this question. The project context showed zero prior plans (sectionCounts.plans = 0), making this a first-plan scenario where 'create' is appropriate. The plan was written with status='active' and all items with status='planned', correctly establishing the initial lifecycle state. No prior active plan needed to be superseded. The audit trail is preserved by creating a new plan entry rather than modifying existing state.
